name: Deoxycholic acid (Kybella)
lead: Deoxycholic acid is a secondary bile acid, produced when gut bacteria modify cholic acid, that normally helps emulsify dietary fats [2][13]. A synthetic, injectable form is sold in the United States as Kybella and in Australia and other markets as Belkyra. It is a prescription cytolytic drug that is injected under the skin of the chin to destroy fat cells, and it is approved for improving the appearance of moderate to severe convexity or fullness caused by submental fat (a "double chin") in adults [1][2].

For looks, the payoff is a cleaner angle between chin and neck: when the fat beneath the chin is reduced, the jawline and profile read as more defined without surgery. Treatment is delivered by a clinician as a series of small injections over several sessions, and the fat cells destroyed are not replaced, so the contour change is intended to be lasting [1][19]. Clinicians quoted in the press link a defined jawline to perceived masculinity, which is one reason men have sought it [23].

The US Food and Drug Administration approved it on 29 April 2015 [2][20]. It was developed as ATX-101 by Kythera Biopharmaceuticals, which Allergan agreed to buy for about $2.1 billion later that year [20]. Two large placebo-controlled phase 3 trials and a three-year follow-up form its research base [1][18][19]. The label says it is not approved for fat outside the submental region [1]; researchers have nonetheless run small studies of the jowls, thighs, flanks and bra-strap area [3][5][7][11].

In looksmaxxing communities it appears mainly as a non-surgical alternative to liposuction for a recessed-looking jawline or neck, and men on looksmax.org have posted about having it done [9]. The label's most common adverse reactions are swelling, bruising, pain, numbness, redness and firmness at the injection site; it also carries warnings for injury to the facial nerve branch that moves the lower lip and for difficulty swallowing [1].

paras: The only approved use is improvement in the appearance of moderate to severe fullness under the chin in adults [1]. Patients see the result as a flatter area beneath the chin and a more visible jaw-neck angle. A 2015 review of male body contouring lists synthetic deoxycholic acid injections among the invasive options for men, alongside liposuction, jawline fillers and implants [4].

Press coverage in 2016 reported plastic surgeons seeing more men aged 30 to 70 requesting it, with one quoted surgeon saying men tend to associate masculinity with a defined jawline and a wide lower face [23]. The same article cited a cost of roughly $750 to $1,500 per session and typically two to four sessions spaced six to ten weeks apart [23]; prices vary by clinic and area.

Because the drug dissolves fat and does not tighten skin, clinicians generally describe it as best suited to people whose fullness is mainly fat rather than loose skin; those with lax skin are sometimes steered towards surgical options. Off-label work reported in the literature includes a small prospective study of jowl fat, studies of upper inner thigh fat, and registered trials for flank fat and bra-strap fat [3][5][7][10][11]. The label says use outside the submental area is not recommended [1].

Beyond appearance, the injection has been registered for study in cutaneous neurofibromas in neurofibromatosis type 1, including one trial comparing it with polidocanol, and in superficial lipoma [14][15][16]. These remain investigational.

Before approval, injections of phosphatidylcholine combined with sodium deoxycholate (PC/DC), marketed as lipodissolve or mesotherapy, were offered in clinics for small fat deposits. According to an account published by the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery, dermatologist Adam Rotunda, then a UCLA resident, and Mike Kolodney studied the mixture from 2003 and found that deoxycholate alone was the active ingredient [21]. A 2005 trial supported its effect on fat tissue, and Kolodney's presentation at a biotechnology conference drew the attention of Kythera, which acquired rights to the compound, then called ATX-101 [21].
Wikipedia notes that deoxycholic acid was also long used as a laboratory detergent for isolating membrane proteins and in gallstone research, uses distinct from the cosmetic injection [2].

The FDA approved Kybella on 29 April 2015, and it became available to trained injectors that summer through a training-based launch [2][20]. On 17 June 2015 Allergan announced it would acquire Kythera for $75 a share, about $2.1 billion, with Kybella the lead product; Kythera had also filed for approval in Switzerland, Canada and Australia [20]. The product is marketed as Belkyra in Australia, where a 2023 registry followed treated patients [22]. A generic became available in the United States in April 2021 [2].

The label describes Kybella as a cytolytic drug that, when injected into submental fat, physically disrupts the cell membrane and causes the cell to lyse [1]. The molecule is a detergent-like steroid with both water-attracting and fat-attracting regions, which underlies its natural role in digestion [13]. The damaged fat cells are cleared by the body over the following months [2].

subs.h: Natural deoxycholic acid in the gut
paras: Naturally occurring deoxycholic acid made by gut bacteria has been studied in relation to colon, liver and metabolic disease, and bile-acid signalling through the FXR receptor [25][13]. Those findings concern the gut metabolite and are not studies of the injected cosmetic product.

The approval rested on two identically designed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (REFINE-1 and REFINE-2) in adults aged 19 to 65 with moderate or severe submental fat and a body mass index of 40 or less. Trial 1 randomized 256 people to Kybella and 250 to placebo; trial 2 randomized 258 and 258; mean age was 49 and 85 percent of participants were women. Participants received up to six treatments at least a month apart [1][18].

The co-primary endpoint required improvement on both clinician and patient rating scales 12 weeks after the last treatment. A one-grade composite response was seen in 70.0 percent of the Kybella group versus 18.6 percent of placebo in trial 1, and 66.5 percent versus 22.2 percent in trial 2; a stricter two-grade response was seen in 13.4 percent versus under 0.1 percent, and 18.6 percent versus 3.0 percent [1]. In an MRI subset of 449 participants, 43 percent of treated participants had a fat-volume reduction of at least 10 percent, against 5 percent on placebo [1]. Presenting the results at the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery meeting, investigator Jean Carruthers reported that patient-rated psychological impact of submental fat also improved more with treatment, with overall satisfaction near 90 percent [18].

A three-year follow-up of 224 REFINE participants (113 treated, 111 placebo) published in Aesthetic Surgery Journal in 2021 reported that the clinician-rated one-grade response was maintained in 86.4 percent versus 56.8 percent at year 1, 90.6 versus 73.8 percent at year 2, and 82.4 versus 65.0 percent at year 3, and that about 74 percent of treated participants who were satisfied at 12 weeks remained satisfied at year 3; the authors reported no new safety signals [19]. A registered 24-month follow-up study of 201 participants was also designed to assess safety and maintenance of effect [8].

A 2023 Australian registry of 86 adults treated with Belkyra reported that 75.0 percent had at least a one-grade improvement on the patient-rated fat scale and that skin laxity did not worsen overall; 22.8 percent of the 79 people in the safety population reported mild, treatment-related adverse events, mostly swelling [22].

Small studies outside the approved area include a prospective study of twelve consecutive patients treated for mild to moderate jowl fat, designed to assess safety and feasibility [3], and a phase I trial of upper inner thigh fat [5]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists small completed phase 4 studies on flank fat, small fatty deformities, bra-strap fat and combinations with triamcinolone [6][7][11][12][17].

In the pooled pivotal trials (513 treated, 506 placebo) the label lists swelling in 87 percent of treated participants (43 percent placebo), hematoma or bruising 72 percent (70), pain 70 (32), numbness 66 (6), redness 27 (18) and induration 23 (3) [1]. Dermatology Times coverage of the trial presentation described most events as mild to moderate and temporary, with fewer than 4 percent withdrawing for adverse events [18].

The label's warnings cover injury to the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve, seen in trials as an asymmetric smile or facial weakness that resolved in all cases (range 1 to 298 days, median 44 days); dysphagia in 2 percent of treated participants (10 of 513), resolving within 1 to 81 days; bleeding and bruising, with caution in people on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy; and alopecia, ulceration, necrosis, nodules and infection at the injection site [1]. It advises avoiding injection near salivary glands, lymph nodes, muscles, arteries and veins [1].

Section 5.5 of the label reports serious reactions after unapproved use outside the submental region, including vision changes with periorbital use and facial paresis or paresthesia [1]. No adequate human pregnancy trials exist; rat studies showed no fetal harm, while rabbit studies showed a missing lung lobe at all doses tested [1]. Safety and effectiveness in children are not established [1].

In looksmaxxing forums, a user describing a genetic submental fat pad that he felt spoiled his side profile posted that a clinician he consulted recommended Kybella over liposuction and said many men attend her clinic for double-chin and jaw work; replies welcomed more cosmetic content on the forum [9]. Another thread asked whether it could be used in the nasolabial fold fat pad as an alternative to filler [10]; the label states that use outside the submental region is not recommended [1].

In December 2023 the FDA warned that unapproved fat-dissolving injections sold at clinics, med spas and online, under names such as Aqualyx, Lipodissolve, Lipo Lab and Kabelline, had been linked to reports of scarring, infections, skin deformities, cysts and painful knots; it noted Kybella as the only approved drug of this kind [24]. Common ingredients in the unapproved products are phosphatidylcholine and sodium deoxycholate [24].
Kybella is prescription-only in the US and EU and Schedule 4 in Australia [2]. A generic version has been sold in the US since April 2021 [2]. Belkyra is the brand used in Australia [22].

Registered studies are examining repeat treatments in cutaneous neurofibromas and a superficial lipoma injection product, and comparisons with polidocanol, alongside further off-label body areas [14][15][16].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the injection is discussed as a minimally invasive alternative to liposuction for the chin and neck, with occasional questions about off-label areas [9][10]. Forum members note that it is one of few clinical procedures posted about there.

claims.claim: Kybella is a good non-surgical alternative to lipo for a small submental fat pad
claims.believers: A poster with a genetic submental fat pad reported that a consulting doctor preferred Kybella to liposuction because the area was small [9].
claims.experts: The FDA label approves the drug for moderate to severe submental fullness in adults, and trials showed significant improvement over placebo, with swelling, bruising, pain and numbness as common reactions [1][18].

claims.claim: It can be used in other areas such as the nasolabial fat pad
claims.believers: A forum thread asked whether it could dissolve nasolabial-area fat instead of using filler [10].
claims.experts: The label states that use outside the submental region is not recommended and reports serious reactions after unapproved use [1]. Small studies have examined jowls and thighs, not this area [3][5].

claims.claim: Results are permanent because treated fat cells do not come back
claims.believers: Proponents describe the destroyed fat cells as gone for good, so the contour change is meant to be lasting.
claims.experts: A three-year follow-up of the pivotal trials found the clinician-rated response maintained in most treated participants at year 3 (82.4 percent versus 65.0 percent on placebo) [19].

claims.claim: It sharpens the jawline for men
claims.believers: Plastic surgeons quoted in the press say men associate a defined jawline with masculinity and seek it for that reason [23].
claims.experts: The trials enrolled mostly women (85 percent) and measured submental fat rating scales rather than jawline definition, so male-specific outcomes were not the primary measure [1].

claims.claim: Any 'fat-dissolving' injection from a spa or website works like Kybella
claims.believers: Unapproved products are sold at clinics, med spas and online under names such as Aqualyx, Lipodissolve and Lipo Lab [24].
claims.experts: The FDA warned in 2023 that unapproved products had caused scarring, infections and deformities and said Kybella is the only approved drug of this type [24].

card.summary: Injectable fat-cell destroyer approved for double chins; works on a small area, with swelling and rare nerve injury.
card.note: Approved only for submental fat; marginal mandibular nerve injury and dysphagia are labelled warnings.

quick.overview:
Deoxycholic acid is a bile acid that the body makes to digest fat. A synthetic version, sold as Kybella, is injected under the chin to destroy fat cells and reduce a double chin. The US FDA approved it in 2015 for adults with moderate to severe submental fullness.

People in looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a lower-downtime alternative to liposuction for the chin and neck, and sometimes ask about using it elsewhere on the face. Off-label use is not recommended on the label and has been tested only in small studies.
quick.mechanism: Injected into fat under the skin, the drug acts as a detergent that disrupts fat-cell membranes so the cells burst. The body then clears the debris over several months.
quick.risks: The label lists swelling, bruising, pain, numbness, redness and hardness as the most common reactions. Warnings include injury to the facial nerve branch controlling the lower lip, trouble swallowing and hair loss in the treated area. It is prescription-only.

chain: Injected deoxycholic acid disrupts submental fat-cell membranes
Treated fat cells die and are cleared over weeks to months
Less fullness under the chin, so a sharper chin-neck angle and jawline
angle.text: Kybella is used by people who want a leaner, more defined profile and who have a fat pad under the chin. After a series of clinic injections, treated fat cells do not return, and the area looks flatter. It reduces fat, not loose skin.
